content: The Butternut tree, scientifically known as Juglans cinerea and sometimes referred to as the White Walnut, is a species of walnut native to the eastern United States and southeastern Canada. Its range extends from southern Quebec westward to Minnesota, southward to northern Alabama, and southwestward to northern Arkansas. This tree is deciduous and typically grows to a height of 20 meters, though it can occasionally reach 30 meters. The trunk diameter ranges from 40 to 80 centimeters, and the bark is light gray in color. The leaves are pinnate, measuring 40 to 70 centimeters in length, and consist of 11 to 17 leaflets. Each leaflet is 5 to 10 centimeters long and 3 to 5 centimeters wide. The entire leaf is covered in fine, downy hairs and exhibits a somewhat brighter, yellow-green hue compared to the leaves of many other tree species. The flowers of the Butternut tree are small and inconspicuous, appearing as yellow-green catkins in the spring, coinciding with the emergence of new leaves. The fruit is a nut that grows in clusters of 2 to 6. Each nut is oblong-ovoid in shape, measuring 3 to 6 centimeters in length and 2 to 4 centimeters in width. The nut is encased in a green husk, which matures and splits open in mid-autumn. The Butternut tree grows rapidly but has a relatively short lifespan for a tree, rarely living beyond 75 years. It is currently under significant threat from a canker disease caused by the fungus Sirococcus clavigignentijuglandacearum. In some regions, this disease has resulted in the death of up to 90% of Butternut trees. Trees that grow in open, isolated conditions appear to have a better chance of surviving the fungal infection compared to those in dense stands or forests. However, the fungus is spread by a wide-ranging vector, meaning that even isolated trees are not completely protected. The nuts of the Butternut tree are commonly used in baking and candy-making due to their oily texture and pleasant flavor. The husks of the nuts are utilized to produce a yellowish dye. The wood of the Butternut tree is lightweight, polishes well, and is highly resistant to rot, though it is much softer than Black Walnut wood. When oiled, the grain of the wood often displays a light appearance. Butternut wood is frequently used in furniture-making and is a preferred material for woodcarvers.
